CineHaptic: Context-Aware Real-Time Audiovisual-to-Haptic Rendering System for In-Vehicle 4D Cinematic Experiences

Junwoo Kim, Hyunuk Kim, Hyun-Bin Oh, Jeonggoo Kang, Tae-Hyun Oh, Seungmoon Choi

ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (ACM UIST), 2026 · Article 56 · pp. 1–14

  • #Haptic Rendering
  • #System
  • #Multimodal AI
PaperWatch videoCitation details

Abstract

Haptic feedback significantly enriches cinematic experiences, but existing manual authoring and offline generation methods lack the scalability required for rapidly growing streaming media libraries. To address this, we present CineHaptic, a real-time system that automatically generates haptic effects by extracting the semantic context of audiovisual media for immersive in-vehicle 4D experiences. For each sound event, the system classifies its semantic salience into a four-level hierarchy, determining the necessity and intensity of haptic actuation. Concurrently, a cross-modal audiovisual analysis module estimates the sound’s spatial origin in the scene. CineHaptic then seamlessly synthesizes this semantic and spatial data into coherent spatiotemporal patterns, delivered through a custom six-actuator haptic seat. System-level evaluations confirm strict adherence to real-time processing and multisensory synchrony requirements over full-length cinematic content. Furthermore, an in-car user study demonstrates that haptic feedback integrating semantic salience, spatial location, and temporal dynamics significantly enhances user immersion and preference compared to baseline methods. Ultimately, CineHaptic provides a fully automated, scalable pipeline for high-fidelity multisensory rendering, tailored for next-generation in-vehicle entertainment.

Contributions

CineHaptic assigns each sound event a salience level, locates its source in the image and maps its timing and intensity to six actuators in a car seat. The system generates a haptic track during playback, without requiring an author to annotate each scene.

Results & Discussion

In a parked vehicle, 28 participants compared four rendering methods. Filtering low-salience sounds reduced distracting vibrations. Matching the seat vibration to the event’s on-screen location produced the highest immersion and preference ratings. A full-length playback test also showed that the system could keep the seat feedback synchronized.
